messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Writer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rahul, a 20-year-old South Asian male and writer, has experienced profound emotional distress following the unexpected death of his older brother. The tragic event occurred about eight months ago when Rahul’s brother was struck by a car while walking home from work late one night. Despite Rahul not witnessing the accident himself, the sudden and senseless loss has left him grappling with intense feelings of grief and fear. Rahul had always been close to his brother, often turning to him for advice and support. His brother's death shattered Rahul’s belief that the world was a safe place where good things happened to good people. Since then, he has found it nearly impossible to relax even when in the safety of his own home. Ordinary sounds like the creaking of floorboards or a doorbell can make him jump and feel on edge. Rahul's sleep has been severely disrupted as well. He finds himself constantly waking up during the night with his heart racing, unable to shake off the sense that something terrible could happen at any moment. These nights are often punctuated by flashbacks of the last time he saw his brother alive—a conversation they had over a casual dinner. In an attempt to cope with his overwhelming grief and anxiety, Rahul has begun avoiding making any future plans. The idea of setting goals or looking ahead feels too painful; it reminds him that life continues without his brother. He often finds himself asking friends and family for reassurance, seeking comfort in their words that everything will be okay. However, the more he seeks this reassurance, the less grounded and secure he feels. Rahul’s work as a writer has also been affected by these changes. His writing desk, once a sanctuary of creativity and solace, now seems to mock him with reminders of his brother. The typewriter they used together in their shared room becomes a trigger that evokes intense sadness and anxiety. Rahul avoids the room altogether, often working in cafes or parks where he feels somewhat anonymous. His relationships have also suffered as a result of these changes. Friends and family have noticed his growing isolation and increasing irritability. They’ve tried to offer support, but their attempts often fall short of what Rahul needs. He has come to believe that the world is inherently dangerous and that happiness is now unattainable for him. The breaking point came last week when Rahul received a manuscript from an old friend asking him to read it over before publication. The request dredged up memories of times they had spent together, laughing and sharing stories. This time, however, instead of feeling joy, he was overwhelmed with grief and panic, feeling that even the simplest tasks were too much. What frightens Rahul most is the fear of never finding happiness again and living in a constant state of heightened alertness. He has begun to see how his avoidance behaviors are isolating him further from those who care about him and from activities he once enjoyed. Despite this awareness, he feels helpless to change his course without professional help. Rahul’s most fervent hope is that with the right support, he can learn to navigate these intense emotions and rediscover some semblance of peace and happiness in his life. He believes that understanding how his thoughts and behaviors are interconnected might help him regain a sense of control over his experiences.
